data.title: Archaeological cultures in Slovakia – a dating chart
data.excerpt: The Lusatian culture, the La Tène period, Hallstatt, the Early and the Late Bronze Age, the Celts, the Roman period — few readers can place these terms on a comprehensible timeline, and such a chart is surprisingly hard to find anywhere. Rudo and Evka had one drawn up with the help of archaeologists for their new book Putovanie po hradoch Slovenských 2; it covers the span from the Eneolithic to the modern era.
data.metaTitle: Archaeological cultures in Slovakia – a dating chart
data.metaDescription: A timeline of the archaeological cultures of Slovakia from the Palaeolithic to the Middle Ages: the Lusatian culture, Hallstatt, La Tène and the Roman period.

mediaTexts.alt: A table of the archaeological cultures and historical periods in Slovakia from the Eneolithic to the modern era

children.text:
Are you still confused about the order in which all the archaeological cultures followed one another in the territory of Slovakia, from the Palaeolithic to the Late Middle Ages? What period do these cultures belong to? How did they overlap with one another? What peoples lived at the time? There are a great many people who get lost in terms such as the Lusatian culture, the La Tène period, Hallstatt, the Early and the Late Bronze Age, the Celts, the Roman period, the Migration Period… and cannot place them even approximately on a comprehensible timeline. 
Just try to look up such a clear table on the internet. You will probably break quite a sweat, and even so you will arrive only at very poor results. You will probably be even more surprised that in the scholarly literature this periodisation was published back in the depths of socialism, and that since then you will not find (at least I have not found it, but perhaps I simply searched badly) any similar specialist article with an “official” periodisation. 
 All the more pleasing, then, was the idea of Rudo Malý and his wife Evka to include such a table (a timeline) in their new book “Putovanie po hradoch Slovenských 2” (Journeying through the Castles of Slovakia 2), which has appeared only recently (and which is selling like hot cakes, so do not hesitate and order it), so that the Slovak reader might gain a better idea of our earliest history. 
He therefore approached archaeologists with a request for help and set to work. The result is this clear table, in which you will find everything you need.

The table shows both the individual periods (the Stone Age, the Bronze Age, the Iron Age etc.) and, within them, all the cultures and known peoples that we are able to recognise. For each period the table also gives the century or the millennium that corresponds to it. Rudo and Evka write about the table:

“Then I had the idea of a graphic, clear presentation of the periods-peoples-cultures that existed in Slovakia. I looked for available materials and found that it is not quite so simple. An archaeologist friend referred me to material that was published in the 1980s. But mind you! That was quite a long time ago and much has changed. …on the website www.hradiska.sk, something in history textbooks, on the web…and I set about working it up. You can see the result on the following page; it covers the period from the Eneolithic to the modern era (-4000 BC to the year 1800). I have added the names, the cultures and the significant peoples. The data have been consulted with an archaeologist. I was warned that “there is more of it” and that it could be divided in more detail for eastern-central-western Slovakia, but I am fully convinced that this form of graphic representation will be enough for you, as it is for me.”

Five years ago the married couple Eva Mladá and Rudolf Mladý published their first book about their journeying through the castles – fortlets – hillforts – fortifications of Slovakia. The book described 520 sites and the success of this publication was surprising for the authors. They do not deal with history in it. It is rather a “baedeker” telling where the individual fortifications are to be found. They went on with their travelling and discovering. To this day they have personally visited over 1,200 fortifications in our beautiful Slovakia, in which they probably hold the record. That led them to publish

, many of which are certainly published publicly for the first time. The whole of Slovakia is truly covered in them. On almost 400 pages you will find clear maps, tables with exact coordinates, elevation, place, district… The main chapter consists of the sites arranged in alphabetical order by the cadastral area in which the fortifications lie. There is also a small map marking the starting point, a description of the route, the difficulty, thousands of the authors’ own photographs, ground plans…

The introduction to the book will also be of interest to many laymen. In it the authors answer frequent questions about the work of archaeologists and of civic associations, or about unconventional methods of investigation used by professional specialists. From their own point of view they also present our “most” records – the highest situated fortifications, the largest ones. But also information about historical inscriptions on rocks, or about dúpence. They have never claimed to be specialists, rather only tourists with “good fitness”, which they needed with that number of sites. Whoever has both volumes will gain the most comprehensive survey of fortifications, one that will probably be hard to surpass. Readers are often surprised at how much unknown or little-known material can be found in their immediate surroundings. When they are asked where they learned about precisely those unknown fortifications, they answer that they are lucky in their friends. A good many archaeologists cheered them on and gave them tips on fortifications. Many are still uninvestigated. Without such help they would never have achieved their goal. Just as a point of interest, in their journeying they drove 93,181 km by car around Slovakia, which is 2.3 times the circumference of the equator. On foot, from the car to the site and back, they covered 2,422 km, which is 5.7 times the straight-line distance from Kremenec to Záhorská Ves. Of course, the number of 1,200 fortifications is not final. Archaeologists work on and “something new” is always discovered. The book is published privately, without sponsors, funds or institutions, in a limited print run.
